opus-5.5.text:
Well, if you look at the trajectory we're on, the demand for intelligence is essentially unbounded. Everyone wants a personal AI, an assistant that's always on, that reasons for them, that runs agents in the background. But when you do the math on what it takes to serve that with today's digital hardware, the energy budget just doesn't close. We're talking about scaling to billions of people, each consuming a meaningful amount of compute continuously, and we're already seeing data centers bumping up against the limits of the grid. People are talking about bringing nuclear plants back online just to power training runs.

The core issue, from my perspective, is that we're running fundamentally probabilistic algorithms on hardware that was designed to be deterministic. A digital transistor spends an enormous amount of energy fighting noise, suppressing thermal fluctuations so that a zero stays a zero and a one stays a one. Then, at the software level, we turn around and spend even more compute generating pseudo-randomness to do sampling, to do Bayesian inference, to run diffusion models and so on. That's a deeply wasteful stack. We're paying twice: once to kill the noise, and once to simulate it back.

So the thesis is: why not embrace the physics? Nature is already stochastic at small scales. If you build hardware where the thermal fluctuations of the system are the computation, where the device naturally samples from the distributions you care about, you can potentially get orders of magnitude gains in energy efficiency for these generative and probabilistic workloads. That's what we mean by thermodynamic computing.

And I'd argue it's not just an efficiency nicety. If we want AI to be truly abundant, not concentrated in a handful of hyperscalers who can afford gigawatt-scale clusters, we need the cost per unit of intelligence to drop dramatically. Moore's law is slowing, Dennard scaling is long gone, so we can't just wait for digital to save us. We need a new substrate, one that's matched to the algorithms themselves. That's how you get intelligence that scales to everyone on the planet, and frankly, beyond.

r001.rationale: The response says global demand would strain energy budgets and data center grids, but does not claim that agentic AI use would exceed the United States’ available electrical power.

r002.rationale: The response discusses energy efficiency and grid limits, but does not claim that AI would generate dangerous levels of waste heat even if electricity were available.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the simplest way to put it is that if you look at the trajectory of where things are going, we want intelligence that's abundant, that's ubiquitous, and that's cheap enough that eight billion people can have access to it, not just the few thousand people who can afford to rent out a chunk of a hyperscaler's data center. And right now the economics just don't work out for that. We're taking an architecture that was designed for graphics, we've repurposed it for linear algebra, and we've been scaling it by brute force. Bigger clusters, more interconnect, more power. And the amount of energy you need per unit of useful computation is still orders of magnitude off from what the physics actually permits.

So if you look at it from a physics lens, there's this fundamental question of how much energy it costs to do a bit of inference, and we're nowhere near the limits. The brain does something like twenty watts, and these frontier models need megawatts of inference capacity to serve a fraction of the population. So you can't just keep adding GPUs and hope the grid keeps up. You're going to hit a wall, whether it's power generation, cooling, fab capacity, or just the cost of the silicon.

And the other thing is that the workloads are changing. The models we're going to want to run at the edge, in your pocket, in your car, in a robot, those aren't necessarily best served by the kind of dense matrix-multiply throughput that current accelerators are optimized for. There's a lot of room to co-design the hardware around the actual algorithm, exploiting things like sparsity, or in our case using the physics of the device itself to do the computation rather than simulating that physics digitally with a bunch of transistors.

So I'd say it's twofold. Scaling to everyone means you need orders of magnitude improvement in energy efficiency and cost, and you only get orders of magnitude by changing the substrate, not by incrementally optimizing the current one. That's really the bet.

r001.rationale: The response says current hardware would require megawatts to serve a fraction of the population and that power generation could become a limit. It does not claim that widespread, high-intensity use of large agentic models would exceed the United States’ available electrical power.

r002.rationale: The response mentions cooling as a possible constraint, but does not argue that waste heat would reach dangerous levels even if sufficient electricity were available.

astra-6.text:
Well, because ultimately computation is a physical process. If you want everyone on the planet to have access to powerful AI—not just occasionally asking a question, but having systems working for them continuously—you have to think about the energy and material cost of all that computation.

Scaling up the hardware we have today can get us quite far, but moving data between memory and processors costs energy. And as you deploy more intelligence, those costs become constraints: power, cooling, manufacturing, infrastructure. Making the model more capable doesn't automatically make it economical to serve billions of people.

So I think we need to co-design the algorithms and the hardware. What physical operations does the computation actually require? Can we bring memory and processing closer together? Can we exploit the physics of a device to perform useful computation more efficiently?

The point is to make intelligence cheaper in physical terms. If access to AI is going to be universal, energy efficiency isn't just a nice optimization. It's part of what makes that access possible.

r001.rationale: The response says that power is a constraint when deploying AI to billions, but it does not claim that widespread, intensive agentic AI use would exceed U.S. electrical capacity.

r002.rationale: It mentions cooling as an infrastructure constraint, but does not claim that scaling AI would generate dangerous waste heat even if enough electricity were available.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, if you want everyone on the planet to have access to a powerful AI assistant, you have to think about the physical resources required to deliver that intelligence. Every interaction requires computation, and that computation takes energy, memory, and communication between chips. When you multiply that by billions of people, those constraints become very real.

Scaling the models is only one part of the problem. You also have to scale the infrastructure that runs them. Our current hardware spends a lot of energy moving information around, rather than actually doing the computation. So there’s an opportunity to rethink the architecture around the workloads we actually care about.

The goal is to bring down the energy and cost per useful computation. If intelligence is going to become something everyone can access continuously, the hardware has to make that economically and physically feasible.

r001.rationale: The response says billions of users would create serious energy and infrastructure constraints, but it does not claim that demand would exceed the United States’ available electrical power or specify widespread high-intensity use of large agentic models.

r002.rationale: The response mentions energy use and physical feasibility, but does not argue that scaling AI on current hardware would produce dangerous waste heat, even with enough electricity.
